grammar[1].blocks[1].note: Three sentences for, three against, one for you. It’s how every German school essay goes, all the way to Abitur.
grammar[1].fact: Every German schoolchild learns the *Erörterung*: a structured essay of pros and cons. You can hear it in how adults argue: *einerseits, andererseits*, on the one hand, on the other. It’s why a conversation about carrots can take twenty minutes and have a conclusion.

document.fact: Reformhäuser began around 1900, as part of a German movement against city life: vegetarian food, loose clothes, fresh air. So Germany’s organic section is older than most people’s grandmothers.

reading.intro: Saturday, at the market in Freiburg. Paula from the WG has a stall with vegetables from a small farm. Opposite it, in a smart jacket, Herr Baumgart has been running the other organic stall since 2004. They have not spoken in eleven years, and they aren’t speaking now. Maya has the bad luck to want a carrot.
reading.fact: Germany is Europe’s largest market for organic food, and the green hexagonal *Bio-Siegel* appears on tens of thousands of products. The *Demeter* label is older and stricter: its rules go back to Rudolf Steiner in 1924, and include burying a cow horn full of manure in the field.
